title: Which group gets the bigger share of guavas?
description: Two groups pool their guavas into one pile each and share them equally. The board adds each pile, divides by the number of children, and compares the two fair shares. Keeko doubts that equal piles must give equal shares.
teaching_notes: One idea: the average is a fair share, the total divided by the number of people sharing it. Watch for children who compare only the two totals and forget the group sizes.

source: Shreyas's group of 5 collected 3, 8, 10, 5 and 4 guavas. Par
video_script.why: The child can find a total but has not yet seen that the same total shared by different numbers of people gives different shares.
video_script.substitution: The two guava piles are equal; only the number of children sharing each pile changes.
video_script.anchor: Two groups of children with their guava piles: a group of five and a group of six
video_script.wrong_answer: both groups get the same share
video_script.wrong_move: compares the two totals and ignores how many children share each pile
video_script.payoff_line: Each member of Leeza's group gets one more guava

final_answer.value: Leeza's group: 6 guavas each against 5, so 1 more each
final_answer.spoken: six guavas each in the first group, one more than in the second group

names.Leeza: leads the guava-picking group of five
names.Jia: leads the second guava-picking group, of six

maths_rules: fair share = total / number of children
6 - 5 = 1 guava more for each member of the first group
video_script.design: Two piles of guavas of the same size; five children round one, six round the other. The board adds, divides and compares.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; two groups of children stand beside two heaps of guavas, five children in one group and six in the other

marks.m1: the title card From your book appears
marks.m2: the group of five and the group of six appear with their names
marks.m3: an equal-sharing arrow circles each heap
marks.m4: a question mark rises over the two groups

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book about two groups picking guavas.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Leeza leads a group of five, and Jia leads a group of six.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Each group will share its guavas equally among its members.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>In which group does each member get the bigger share?

beats.on_screen: the two groups stay on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child who is thinking

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: each group tips its guavas into one heap; the heap is then dealt out equally, one guava at a time, to the children of that group

marks.g1: all the guavas of a group slide into one heap
marks.g2: the heap is dealt out equally to the children
marks.g3: the label fair share appears on one child's guavas

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>First, each group puts all its guavas into one heap.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>Then the heap is dealt out equally among the children of that group.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>The number of guavas each child gets is called the fair share.

beats.on_screen: Given: Leeza's group of 5 picked 3, 8, 10, 5, 4 guavas; Jia's group of 6 picked 5, 4, 6, 3, 4, 8 guavas

marks.given: the two rows of guava counts are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the first group of five picked three, eight, ten, five and four guavas.
The second group of six picked five, four, six, three, four and eight guavas.

beats.on_screen: To find: the group whose members get the bigger fair share

marks.find: the words fair share are underlined

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the group whose members get the bigger fair share.

beats.on_screen: Step 1, add to get each total: 3 + 8 + 10 + 5 + 4 = 30 guavas; 5 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 4 + 8 = 30 guavas

marks.s1: the first row of numbers is added to its total
marks.s2: the second row of numbers is added to its total

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, add the guavas of each group to get its total, because the whole heap is shared.
<bookmark mark='s2'/>The first group has thirty guavas, and the second group also has thirty.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, fair share = total ÷ number of children: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 guavas; 30 ÷ 6 = 5 guavas

marks.d1: the rule fair share = total ÷ number of children is written
marks.d2: 30 is divided by the 5 children of the first group
marks.d3: 30 is divided by the 6 children of the second group

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Step two, divide each total by the number of children, because the heap is shared equally.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>Thirty divided by five gives six guavas for each child of the first group.
<bookmark mark='d3'/>Thirty divided by six gives five guavas for each child of the second group.

marks.c1: the two fair shares sit side by side
marks.c2: the gap between 6 and 5 is marked

narration: <bookmark mark='c1'/>Step three, compare the two fair shares.
<bookmark mark='c2'/>Six is more than five, and six take away five leaves one.

beats.on_screen: Answer: each member of Leeza's group gets 6 guavas, 1 more guava than in Jia's group
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each member of Leeza's group gets one more guava.
The fair share is six guavas in the first group and five in the second.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's thought bubble shows the two heaps of 30 with an equals tick; the five children and the six children then light up and the tick is struck through

marks.doubt: the bubble with the two equal heaps appears
marks.fix: the five children and the six children light up

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks both groups get the same share, because both have thirty guavas.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the heaps are equal, and the groups are not.
Five children share the first heap, and six share the second.
<bookmark mark='idea'/>The same heap cut among more children gives each one a smaller share.
